question.text: This man served as president of Princeton from 1902 to 1910 before being elected U.S. president in 1912.
question.clue: Henry Cabot Lodge objected to this man's proposed mutual defense clause, Article X, which failed to be ratified in the U.S. Senate.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about famous campaign slogans.
swap.text: This 28th U.S. President first elected in 1912 ran on the slogan "he kept us out of war" to win reelection in 1916. Ironically, this man entered the war after the sinking of the Lusitania.
swap.clue: McReynolds prevented an official photo of the Court from being taken because he refused to sit next to a Jew, namely another one of this President's nominees, Louis Brandeis.

question.leadin: Answer the following about scandals in American presidential history.
question.text: This scandal during the Harding administration dealt with the fixing of oil prices and saw the Secretary of the Interior, Albert Fall, convicted of conspiracy and bribery.
question.clue: It partially concerned an area in Elk Hills, California which had originally been under the jurisdiction of Secretary of the Navy Edwin Denby.

swap.text: Woodrow Wilson created this set of proposals, including freedom of the seas and self-determination, for the postwar world. They were mostly ignored in actual treaties.
swap.clue: This idea included the mandate that international relations be conducted in the public view, as well as the outline of the foundation of the League of Nations.

question.text: This Lithuanian-born anarchist published the periodical Mother Earth and was the lover of Alexander Berkman, who tried to assassinate Henry Clay Frick during the Homestead Strike.
question.clue: She was boycotted by the British left after discussing her horror with Leninism in My Disillusionment in Russia, and her other writings include the periodical Mother Earth.

swap.leadin: Answer these questions about Progressive Era jurisprudence.
swap.text: This first Jewish justice to serve on the Supreme Court worked on Muller v. Oregon, where he submitted a namesake brief, which heavily relied on social statistics.
swap.clue: He also attacked trusts and monopolies in Other People's Money, and How the Bankers Use It.

question.text: Later, as governor of Pennsylvania, Pinchot supported and helped implement this policy. The Volstead Act enacted this policy.
question.clue: A hatchet was used in activism for this policy by Carrie Nation.

swap.leadin: William Boehner was killed by a bomb intended for the namesake of these events.
swap.text: Name these events led by a namesake Attorney General that unlawfully detained thousands of suspected left-wingers and anarchists during the First Red Scare.
swap.clue: Some targets of these events, which were led by a man nicknamed the "Fighting Quaker,"were placed on the ship Buford, nicknamed the "Soviet Ark."

question.text: Neither Wilson nor this opponent of his in the 1916 election campaigned for Prohibition. Though he was never President, this man did serve as Chief Justice of the Supreme Court and as Governor of New York.
question.clue: He replaced Bainbridge Colby as Secretary of State and chaired the Washington Naval Conference.

swap.leadin: Identify these charitable organizations from a description of their founders.
swap.text: Founded on Halsted Street in 1889 by Ellen Gates Starr and Jane Addams, this settlement served as community center and, sometimes, home for the neighborhood poor.
swap.clue: Its biggest financial backer was Mary Rozet Smith, and one of its leading members was the first director of the Children's Bureau, Julia Lathrop.

question.text: This man, who served as US Attorney General from 1919 to 1921, tried to ferret out communists and socialists by arresting and deporting thousands in his namesake raids.
question.clue: Acting Secretary of Labor Louis Post undid many of this man's actions, which included a crackdown on the Union of Russian Workers for producing an anarchist manifesto.

swap.leadin: Name some failed presidential candidates from the twentieth century.
swap.text: This co-founder of the IWW ran from prison in 1920, the fourth time he was the candidate of the Socialist Party of America and the fifth time he ran overall.
swap.clue: This man later helped found a political party on whose ticket he ran five times.

question.text: As part of his Square Deal, Roosevelt strengthened the Interstate Commerce Commission through both the Hepburn Act and this act, which gave the ICC greater authority to stop railroads from granting rebates to favored customers. Its namesake would later co-sponsor another regulatory bill with James Robert Mann.

swap.text: Mencken was represented by lawyers from this organization that, under the leadership of Roger Nash Baldwin, was also involved in the free speech cases Scopes, Gitlow v. New York, and US v. One Book Called Ulysses.
swap.clue: Helen Keller, a student of Perkins-trained Anne Sullivan, was a co-founder of this nonprofit, which financed the defense of teacher John T. Scopes in the Scopes Monkey Trial.

question.leadin: This period is considered to have ended with the "switch in time that saved nine."
question.text: Name this period during which the Supreme Court took an activist role in striking down anti-business legislation. This era is named for a 1905 case which overturned a law limiting working hours for bakers.
question.answerHtml: Lochner era [prompt on Lochner v. New York by asking “which party of the lawsuit names the period?”]
question.clue: During the later years of this 40-year period, its policies were championed by Butler, McReynolds, Sutherland, and Van Devanter, collectively known as the Four Horsemen.

swap.leadin: This magazine sent Willa Cather to research the life of Mary Baker Eddy.
swap.text: Name this magazine that also published definitive biographies of Napoleon and Abraham Lincoln. This magazine sponsored Ida Tarbell to write a 1904 history that includes interviews with her father and with tycoon Henry H. Rogers.
swap.clue: This periodical ceased after it was combined with The Smart Set to create The New Smart Set.

question.text: According to Adamic, one of the key players in California's "healing industry" was this evangelist, who converted an abandoned church in Echo Park into the Angelus Temple.
question.clue: Earlier, she had travelled the country with her mother in a special car which had the messages "Where Will You Spend Eternity" and "Jesus Is Coming Soon" painted on it.

swap.text: Domestically, support for Kellogg-Briand was led by this man, then Chair of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.

question.leadin: Answer some questions about the most ineffectual of foreign policies, Dollar Diplomacy, FTPE.
question.text: Much of the formulation of the policy was done by this Secretary of State under Taft. He also notably prosecuted some trusts as Attorney General under Teddy Roosevelt.
question.clue: This senator from Pennsylvania who also names a resolution with Porter that ended US involvement in World War I. He most famously served as Taft's Secretary of State after some controversy about his salary.

swap.leadin: Name these things about the policy of "dollar diplomacy," FTP each.
swap.text: The policy's strongest practitioner was this man, who resigned as a senator from Pennsylvania in 1909 to become William Howard Taft's secretary of state.
swap.clue: When William Howard Taft tried to appoint this man Secretary of State, he was briefly considered ineligible because he had served in Congress when it voted a pay raise for the position. He was confirmed after the first "Saxbe fix" temporarily lowered his salary to the pre-raise level.
